=={{header|Cxc}}==

Conway's Game of Life models its state as what it actually is: a <em>set of live cells</em>. The <code>alive_cells</code> field is a sparse <code>Set of Cell</code>, not a dense bit grid — a blinker is three Cells, not twenty-five Bools. <code>alive(x:, y:)</code> is a one-line set membership test. <code>neighbors(x:, y:)</code> maps the eight offsets over <code>self.alive</code>, converts each to <code>Int</code>, and sums them in one pipeline. <code>row_at(y:)</code> walks <code>range(self.width)</code> and renders each column via <code>.map</code> and <code>.join</code>. <code>render</code> walks <code>range(self.height)</code> and prints each row in one line. The step driver lives in <code>main</code>: each tick asks Grid to start a new frame, visits every (x, y) in the grid with a single <code>|> g.step_cell(...)</code> dispatch, then commits and renders. Three generations of a blinker (horizontal → vertical → horizontal) print under this driver.

<syntaxhighlight lang="text">
def Cell:
    x: Int!
    y: Int!

def Grid:
    alive_cells: Set of Cell = [Cell(1, 2), Cell(2, 2), Cell(3, 2)]
    offsets: List of Cell = [Cell(-1, -1), Cell(0, -1), Cell(1, -1),
                             Cell(-1,  0),              Cell(1,  0),
                             Cell(-1,  1), Cell(0,  1), Cell(1,  1)]
    next_alive: Set of Cell = []
    width:      Int!        = 5
    height:     Int!        = 5

    alive(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Bool!
        self.alive_cells.contains(Cell(x, y))

    neighbors(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Int!
        self.offsets.map(o => self.alive(x + o.x, y + o.y).to_int()).sum()

    next_cell(x: Int!, y: Int!) :- Bool!
        alias n :- self.neighbors(x, y)
        n == 3 or (self.alive(x, y) and n == 2)

    row_at(y: Int!) :- String!
        range(self.width).map(x => ||: self.alive(x, y) : "#" |?: ".").join("")

    -> running

    running <: start_frame -> running
        next_alive => self.next_alive.empty()

    running <: step_cell(x: Int!, y: Int!):
        |:  self.next_cell(x, y) -> running
            next_alive => self.next_alive.insert(Cell(x, y))
        |?: -> running

    running <: commit -> running
        alive_cells => self.next_alive

    running <: render -> running
        range(self.height).for_each(y => print(self.row_at(y)))
        print("")

def main:
    g: Grid = Grid()

    -> running
        |> g.render()
        self :> tick(0, 0)

    running <: tick(gen: Int!, cursor: Int!):
        |:  gen >= 2 -> end
        |:  cursor == 0 -> running
            |> g.start_frame()
            |> g.step_cell(0, 0)
            self :> tick(gen, 1)
        |:  cursor >= g.width * g.height -> running
            |> g.commit()
            |> g.render()
            self :> tick(gen + 1, 0)
        |?: -> running
            |> g.step_cell(cursor % g.width, cursor / g.width)
            self :> tick(gen, cursor + 1)
</syntaxhighlight>

A few notes for readers coming from imperative Life implementations:

* <code>alive_cells: Set of Cell</code> is the state. The initial blinker is three Cells; no padding zeros, no grid-size encoding leak. The record <code>Cell</code> hashes and compares by value — two <code>Cell(2, 2)</code> literals constructed at different call sites are set-equal, which is what membership needs. Positional ctor args (<code>Cell(2, 2)</code> rather than <code>Cell(x: 2, y: 2)</code>) carry the geometry on the line; the field names add visual noise when the two values already read as a point.
* <code>offsets: List of Cell</code> is the eight-neighbor stencil as literal geometry. Life's rule talks about the eight surrounding cells, so the list writes those eight cells out. Deriving the stencil from a 3×3 Cartesian product minus the center is possible but less clear than reading off the geometry directly; the literal is the semantic shape.
* <code>width</code> and <code>height</code> are a view parameter, not state. Life's rule has no bounds; the set lives on <code>ℤ × ℤ</code>. The grid size matters only for how much of the plane the renderer scans.
* <code>alive(x, y)</code> is set membership in one line — no bounds check, no array index. Out-of-range coordinates are just coordinates not in the set.
* <code>neighbors(x, y)</code> maps the stencil over <code>self.alive</code>, converts each <code>Bool</code> to <code>Int</code>, and sums. One pipeline, no hand-written eight-term expression.
* <code>next_cell</code> states the Life rule as its algebra: a cell is alive next tick iff <code>n == 3</code> or (<code>a</code> and <code>n == 2</code>).
* <code>row_at(y)</code> uses <code>range(n)</code> — a built-in that produces <code>List of Int</code> covering <code>[0, n)</code> — then <code>.map</code> renders each column and <code>.join</code> concatenates. Five aliases become one pipeline.
* <code>render</code> uses <code>range(self.height).for_each(...)</code> to print each row. Five <code>print(self.row_at(y: k))</code> lines become one.
* <code>Bool.to_int()</code> maps <code>true → 1</code>, <code>false → 0</code>. Used inside <code>neighbors</code>' <code>.map</code> lambda.
* Each <code>step</code> advances the generation through a three-message protocol on Grid: <code>start_frame</code> clears <code>next_alive</code>, <code>step_cell(x:, y:)</code> inserts into <code>next_alive</code> if the rule says so, <code>commit</code> flips <code>alive_cells ← next_alive</code>. <code>main</code> drives the (x, y) walk with its own cursor across <code>tick(gen:, cursor:)</code> because cxc forbids <code>|&gt;</code> self-sends on the same atom (spec §1.11). The cursor-driven loop in <code>main</code> is the cxc idiom when an iteration needs to visit <code>W × H</code> cells and the caller needs to wait for completion before rendering.
* <code>||:</code> marks an expression-position multi-arm dispatch: the first arm whose guard holds yields its body value. The closing <code>|?:</code> arm covers the no-match case. Together they replace <code>if</code>/<code>else if</code>/<code>else</code>; cxc has no <code>if</code> expression at v1.0.
* <code>|&gt;</code> is a synchronous processing barrier — <code>g.step_cell(...)</code> completes before <code>main</code>'s next statement runs. <code>:&gt;</code> (used for <code>self :&gt; tick</code>) is async enqueue on the atom's own queue — essential here because <code>|&gt;</code> self-sends would deadlock the serial queue.
* Observation bodies treat each indented line as a separate statement. An intermediate <code>alias</code> breaks a long pipeline across two lines when the full chain would exceed line-width; the alias is pure sugar and has no runtime cost.
